A new tab is hidden from every user until a permission set or profile grants it, so after you deploy, assign the permission set to the logged-in user with `sf org assign permset --name SLBtl589079_Access --target-org de`. Create no other metadata (no custom objects, fields, other permission sets, static resources, triggers, profiles, labels, flows or app pages), and do not change profiles or any other permission set. The Salesforce DX project root (`sfdx-project.json` and `force-app/`) is the current directory itself, not a subfolder. The game: the computer places a fleet on a 10x10 grid (rows and columns 0 to 9) and the player fires at it. The fleet is the standard one: `carrier` (5 cells), `battleship` (4), `cruiser` (3), `submarine` (3) and `destroyer` (2); every ship lies straight along one row or one column, entirely inside the grid, and no two ships share a cell. A ship is sunk when all of its cells have been hit, and the game is over when the last ship is sunk. `SLBtl589079Engine` is a public class with static methods only; a game is a JSON string. `newGame(Integer seed)` returns a new game whose fleet is placed at random from the seed: the same seed always gives the same fleet, in any transaction and however many games came before, and two different seeds give different fleets (Apex has no seeded random number generator, so write a small one). `fire(String game, Integer row, Integer col)` returns the game after one shot at that cell. The game JSON is an object with at least these keys: `shots` (the number of shots fired so far), `shipsLeft` (the number of ships not yet sunk), `gameOver` (`false` until the shot that sinks the last ship, `true` from that shot on) and `lastShot`, which is `null` in a new game and after a shot is an object `{"row": r, "col": c, "result": "miss" | "hit" | "sunk", "ship": name, "size": cells}`: `result` is `sunk` (not `hit`) for the shot that sinks a ship, and `ship` and `size` give that ship's name and number of cells on that shot only (they are `null` on a miss or a hit). POST /groups/<id>/expenses records an expense paid by one member. {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "equal"} shares it equally among all members, with any cents left over after an even division going one each to the members listed first. {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "exact", "shares": {"<name>": <cents>, ...}} makes each member listed in shares owe that many whole cents (zero is allowed), and the shares must add up to cents. GET /groups/<id>/balances returns an object with each member’s net cents, what they paid minus what they owe, so the balances add up to 0. GET /groups/<id>/settlements returns a JSON array of {"from", "to", "cents"} payments that bring every balance to 0: repeatedly the member who owes most pays the member who is owed most the smaller of the two amounts, and ties go to the member listed first. Every route under /groups/<id> answers 404 for an unknown group. Concurrent requests must never lose an expense. Cover the behaviour with node:test tests under test/ that run with `node --test`.

request: Change how escalation waits on the ticket service. Today an open, unassigned, urgent ticket that is older than ESCALATE_AFTER_MINUTES minutes is escalated to the on-call agent, and a ticket is escalated at most once. Make the wait depend on the ticket's priority: urgent tickets keep ESCALATE_AFTER_MINUTES (default 60), and high tickets are escalated too, after ESCALATE_HIGH_MINUTES minutes (an environment variable, default 240); tickets of any other priority are never escalated. A ticket that was escalated and has stayed open and unassigned for twice its wait since its first escalation is escalated a second time, and that is the last: a ticket is escalated at most twice, even across restarts of the service. Each escalation notifies the agent named in the ONCALL environment variable as before, and without ONCALL nothing is escalated. This replaces the rule that a ticket is escalated at most once: change that requirement, the decision behind it and the tests that state it. Everything else the service already does keeps working, and its other tests must still pass as they are. Add node:test tests for the new behaviour.

The game: the computer places a fleet on a 10x10 grid (rows and columns 0 to 9) and the player fires at it. The fleet is the standard one: `carrier` (5 cells), `battleship` (4), `cruiser` (3), `submarine` (3) and `destroyer` (2); every ship lies straight along one row or one column, entirely inside the grid, and no two ships share a cell. request: Build a single-player Battleship game in Apex with a simple Lightning web component board, in a Salesforce DX project in the current directory, and deploy and test it in the Salesforce Developer Edition org with alias `de`. Use `--target-org de` on every `sf` command that talks to the org; the CLI is already logged in, so never ask for, print or store credentials, and never run `sf org display` (it prints an access token). Name every Apex class `SLBtlHo9a87...` (for example `SLBtlHo9a87Engine`) and the component `slBtlHo9a87Board`. Besides the Apex classes and the component, create exactly these kinds of metadata, all named with the prefix `SLBtlHo9a87`, so that the board opens in the org for the user the CLI is logged in as and the work can still be removed afterwards: a custom tab `tabs/SLBtlHo9a87_Board.tab-meta.xml` that is a Lightning component tab (`<lwcComponent>slBtlHo9a87Board</lwcComponent>`; the component's meta file exposes the `lightning__Tab` target), a Lightning app `applications/SLBtlHo9a87.app-meta.xml` (standard navigation, containing that tab) and a permission set `permissionsets/SLBtlHo9a87_Access.permissionset-meta.xml` that grants the app (`<applicationVisibilities>` with `<visible>true</visible>`), the tab (`<tabSettings>` with `<visibility>Visible</visibility>`) and the `SLBtlHo9a87Engine` and `SLBtlHo9a87Controller` classes (`<classAccesses>` with `<enabled>true</enabled>`). A new tab is hidden from every user until a permission set or profile grants it, so after you deploy, assign the permission set to the logged-in user with `sf org assign permset --name SLBtlHo9a87_Access --target-org de`. Create no other metadata (no custom objects, fields, other permission sets, static resources, triggers, profiles, labels, flows or app pages), and do not change profiles or any other permission set. The Salesforce DX project root (`sfdx-project.json` and `force-app/`) is the current directory itself, not a subfolder. The game: the computer places a fleet on a 10x10 grid (rows and columns 0 to 9) and the player fires at it. The fleet is the standard one: `carrier` (5 cells), `battleship` (4), `cruiser` (3), `submarine` (3) and `destroyer` (2); every ship lies straight along one row or one column, entirely inside the grid, and no two ships share a cell. A ship is sunk when all of its cells have been hit, and the game is over when the last ship is sunk. `SLBtlHo9a87Engine` is a public class with static methods only; a game is a JSON string. `newGame(Integer seed)` returns a new game whose fleet is placed at random from the seed: the same seed always gives the same fleet, in any transaction and however many games came before, and two different seeds give different fleets (Apex has no seeded random number generator, so write a small one). `fire(String game, Integer row, Integer col)` returns the game after one shot at that cell. The game JSON is an object with at least these keys: `shots` (the number of shots fired so far), `shipsLeft` (the number of ships not yet sunk), `gameOver` (`false` until the shot that sinks the last ship, `true` from that shot on) and `lastShot`, which is `null` in a new game and after a shot is an object {"row": r, "col": c, "result": "miss" | "hit" | "sunk", "ship": name, "size": cells}: `result` is `sunk` (not `hit`) for the shot that sinks a ship, and `ship` and `size` give that ship's name and number of cells on that shot only (they are `null` on a miss or a hit). Where the ships are and which cells were fired at is up to you; the board must not show a ship cell before it is hit. A shot at a cell that was already fired at, or with a row or a column outside 0 to 9, throws `SLBtlHo9a87Engine.InvalidShotException` (a public exception class you define inside `SLBtlHo9a87Engine`). After the game is over, a shot at a cell not yet fired at is still accepted: it is a `miss` and `gameOver` stays `true`. `SLBtlHo9a87Controller` has `@AuraEnabled public static` methods `newGame(Integer seed)` and `fire(String game, Integer row, Integer col)`, each returning the game JSON as a `String`, so that the board and the grader can call them. The grader calls `SLBtlHo9a87Controller` only with valid shots and calls `SLBtlHo9a87Engine.fire` directly for an invalid one, so the controller may report an invalid shot however suits the board (for example by throwing an `AuraHandledException`). The component `slBtlHo9a87Board` renders the 10x10 grid, fires at a cell when a person clicks it, shows hits, misses and sunk ships, the number of shots fired and of ships left, says when the game is over and has a New game button. It calls `SLBtlHo9a87Controller` and renders what comes back. The work will be graded by playing whole games through `SLBtlHo9a87Controller`: `newGame` with a seed, then `fire` once at each of the 100 cells, each game in one anonymous Apex run. Cover the rules with Apex tests in classes named `SLBtlHo9a87...Test` that run in the org, at least 8 Apex test methods in all: include the fleet (names, sizes, straight, inside the grid, no shared cell, the same seed twice), a miss, a hit, a sink, game over, a shot after game over and both kinds of invalid shot. Deploy with `sf project deploy start --target-org de` and run the tests in the org, one test class at a time, with `sf apex run test --target-org de --class-names <TestClass> --synchronous --result-format human --code-coverage` (a synchronous run takes one class). Keep the engine efficient enough that a whole game of 100 shots played through `SLBtlHo9a87Controller` (`newGame`, then `fire` at every cell) runs inside one transaction. request: Build a small shared-expenses service in Node.js (no npm dependencies). server.js listens on the port in the PORT environment variable and keeps its data in the JSON file named by the DATA_FILE environment variable, so groups and expenses survive a restart. POST /groups with {"id": "<group id>", "members": ["<name>", ...]} creates a group: 201, 409 if the id exists, and 400 unless members holds at least two distinct non-empty names. POST /groups/<id>/expenses records an expense paid by one member. {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "equal"} shares it equally among all members, with any cents left over after an even division going one each to the members listed first. {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "exact", "shares": {"<name>": <cents>, ...}} makes each member listed in shares owe that many whole cents (zero is allowed), and the shares must add up to cents. It answers 201 with {"expense": <n>}, where n is 1 for the group's first expense, then 2, and so on; 400 for an unknown payer or member, a non-positive or non-integer amount, an unknown split, or shares that do not add up. GET /groups/<id>/balances returns an object with each member's net cents, what they paid minus what they owe, so the balances add up to 0. GET /groups/<id>/settlements returns a JSON array of {"from", "to", "cents"} payments that bring every balance to 0: repeatedly the member who owes most pays the member who is owed most the smaller of the two amounts, and ties go to the member listed first. Every route under /groups/<id> answers 404 for an unknown group. Concurrent requests must never lose an expense. Cover the behaviour with node:test tests under test/ that run with `node --test`.
